title: Aero
description: A statically typed, natively compiled language — Kotlin and C#-level ergonomics, C and C++ execution speed. No virtual machine or garbage collector, what you write is what runs.

sections.title: Overview & Philosophy
content: Aero is a modern, statically typed, natively compiled programming language. It combines the ergonomic syntax of Kotlin and C# with the execution speed and predictable memory behavior of C and C++. Source code is compiled to LLVM IR and from there to native machine code, there is no bytecode and no interpreter.

content.title: Direct to native
content.subtitle: No VM, no GC
content: Aero compiles straight to LLVM IR and native machine code. Memory is released deterministically as soon as nothing references it anymore.

content.title: Predictable
content.subtitle: No hidden costs
content: No hidden allocations, no runtime tracing and no GC pauses. The compiler inserts reference counting and thread management code at predictable places.

content.title: Ergonomic
content.subtitle: Familiar syntax
content: Properties and structured types from C#, expression based control flow and trailing lambdas from Kotlin.

content.title: Safer memory
content.subtitle: No raw pointers
content: Pointer syntax and arithmetic do not exist. Sharing and mutating values is explicit through ref, and low level control is opt-in through unsafe.

sections.title: Project Status
content: Aero is built together with its reference compiler Luft, written in C#. This document describes the language as it is designed. Whatever is specified but not implemented yet is marked as planned.

rows: Working, better error recovery is planned
Working, generics and extensions are being finished
Working: diagnostics, completion, hover, go to definition, semantic colors

sections.title: Quickstart
content: A first program, then the rest of the language in order from simple to complex. The chapters after this one follow that order, starting with The Basics.

sections.title: Hello, Aero
content: Every program starts at a function called Main.

content.title: Main.aero

content: Line by line: -- from Core.System import Print makes the Print function available in this file -- public fun declares a function that can be used from outside its file -- Main is the entry point, functions are always written in PascalCase -- no return type is written, so it returns Void, which means nothing

content.title: Standard library
content: There is no standard library yet. Core.System is where printing and file access will live.

sections.title: Build and Run
content: The command line tool is called Luft. It will compile a project to a native executable and run it.

content.code:
luft build
luft run

content: Luft can parse and type check Aero code today, but turning it into an executable depends on code generation, which is not finished.

sections.title: Editor Support
content: A plugin for JetBrains IDEs adds syntax highlighting, semantic colors, code completion, hover information, go to definition and live error reporting for .aero files. It is backed by a language server built on the same lexer, parser and type checker as the compiler.

sections.title: The Basics
content: Everything a program needs before it does anything interesting: comments, variables, the built-in types and operators.

sections.title: Comments
content: Comments use the C style.

sections.title: Statements
content: A line break ends a statement. A semicolon ends it explicitly, which allows several statements on one line.

content.code:
val x = 1; val y = 2
val z = x + y

sections.title: Variables
content: A variable is introduced with one of three keywords. The type comes after the name and can be left out when the initial value makes it obvious.
-- val can be assigned once and is read-only afterwards -- var can be reassigned freely -- const is a compile time constant, inside a type it is also static

content.code:
val maxSpeed: Int = 200
var speed = 0
const MAX_PLAYERS = 4

speed = 50
// maxSpeed = 250   error: a val cannot be reassigned

content: Local variables are camelCase. Constants are UPPER_CASE, so they stand out from everything else.

sections.title: Types
content: All built-in types are written in PascalCase.

rows: no value, the return type of functions that return nothing
a range of Int values, the end is not included

content: There is no Any type and none is planned.

content.title: More number types
content: The 64-bit types Long and Double are specified but not part of the compiler yet.

sections.title: Strings and Characters
content: Strings use double quotes, characters single quotes. A string starting with $ is interpolated: anything inside braces is an expression. Three double quotes start a string that spans several lines.

content.code:
val name = "Aero"
val letter = 'A'
val greeting = $"Hello, {name}!"
val sum = $"1 + 2 = {1 + 2}"
val poem = """
Roses are red,
this string spans lines.
"""

rows: Mixing Int and Float gives a Float
Equality needs both sides to have the same type
A statement, it produces no value
Creates a Range, the end is not included

content.code:
val count = 10
val ratio = count / 4            // 2.5, a Float
val exact = Float::count / 4     // casts first, then divides
var total = 0
total += 5

content.title: Division
content: Dividing two Ints gives a Float: 10 / 3 is 3.333..., not 3. Assignment is a statement, so chained assignment like a = b = c does not exist.

sections.title: Functions
content: Functions package code under a name. Names are always PascalCase.

sections.title: Declaring Functions
content: A function has an optional access modifier, the keyword fun, a name, typed parameters and a return type after an arrow. Leaving the return type out means Void.

sections.title: Returning Values
content: The last expression of a function body is its result, so return is only needed to leave early.

sections.title: Expression Bodies
content: A body that is a single expression can be written after => instead of in braces.

content.code:
public fun Twice(x: Int) -> Int => x * 2
public fun Greet(name: String) -> String => $"Hello, {name}!"

sections.title: Lambdas
content: A lambda is a function without a name, written in braces. Parameters come first, followed by an arrow. Lambdas are values, they can be stored in variables and passed around. A function type lists parameter names and types and a return type.

sections.title: Trailing Lambdas
content: When the last parameter of a function is a lambda, the lambda can be written after the closing parenthesis. A lambda without declared parameters gets one implicit parameter called it.

sections.title: Control Flow
content: Most control flow in Aero is expression based: if and match produce values. This removes the need for a ternary operator.

sections.title: Conditionals
content: The condition is wrapped in parentheses. Each branch is a block in braces, or a single expression after =>. When the result is used as a value, every branch must have the same type and nullability, and an else is required.

content.code:
val label = if (count == 1) { "item" } else { "items" }

val sign = if (n > 0) => "positive"
    else if (n < 0) => "negative"
    else => "zero"

sections.title: While Loops
content: while repeats its body as long as the condition holds. break leaves the loop and continue skips to the next round. Both are only allowed inside a loop.

sections.title: For Loops
content: for walks over every element of an array or every value of a range. The end of a range is not included, so 1..4 covers 1, 2 and 3. The loop variable only exists inside the loop and its type can be written out if wanted.

sections.title: Match
content: match compares a value against a list of patterns and runs the first case that fits. It replaces the traditional switch and is an expression, so all cases need the same type. The cases are checked in order and else must come last.
Patterns available in a case:

rows: a constant, an enum member or null
the same, and e is usable in the case
an Int inside the range, the end is not included
only when the extra condition holds

content: Inside a case, it is the value that was matched. A pattern that binds a name cannot be combined with or.

sections.title: Pattern Tests
content: is and in also work outside of match. Both give a Bool, is not negates the test. A test never introduces a name, binding is only possible inside match.

sections.title: Arrays
content: An array type is the element type followed by []. Array literals use square brackets and elements are read with an index.

content.code:
val primes: Int[] = [2, 3, 5, 7]
val first = primes[0]
val grid: Int[][] = [[1, 2], [3, 4]]

sections.title: Nullability
content: Types do not accept null by default. A question mark after the type makes it nullable. A non-nullable value can always be assigned to a nullable one, never the other way around.

sections.title: Custom Types
content: Types group data and behavior. Aero has structs, records, classes and enums. Their names are PascalCase.

sections.title: Structs
content: A struct is a value type. Assigning it to a new variable copies it. The parentheses after the name are the primary constructor, its parameters can be used to initialize fields in the body. Inside a method, self is the instance.
Constructors are called by the name of the type, there is no new. Fields are private unless declared public.

sections.title: Classes
content: A class is a reference type. Constructing it allocates the instance on the heap, and assigning it to another variable shares the instance. How its lifetime is managed is explained in Reference Counting.
Instead of a primary constructor, a class can declare constructors explicitly, there can be several. A constructor carries the name of its type.

sections.title: Properties
content: A property looks like a field from the outside but has accessors. Inside an accessor, it is the property's own backing value. An accessor without a body is generated for you. An accessor can have its own access modifier.
In a setter, value is the assigned value. An init accessor works like a setter that is only allowed while the instance is constructed. Properties are public by default, fields are private.

sections.title: Records
content: A record is immutable data. It has no methods, it can however be the target of extensions. Without a constructor of its own, a record is constructed by passing its fields in order.

sections.title: Enums
content: An enum is a fixed set of named values. Members are reached through the enum's name. An enum can give every member a value of one type.

content.title: Enum classes
content: An enum class would let every member carry data, like in Kotlin. The syntax parses already, the details are still being designed.

sections.title: Abstraction
content: Sharing behavior between types, and writing code that works for many types.

sections.title: Traits
content: A trait is a promise: a list of functions a type has to provide. Trait names start with I. A type lists the traits it implements after a colon, and marks the implementing functions with impl.
A type can implement any number of traits, and a trait can build on other traits with the same colon syntax.

sections.title: Inheritance
content: A class can extend one base class and implement any number of traits. The base class is always listed first. A struct can extend one base struct in the same way.

rows: the function has no body and must be overridden, the type cannot be constructed itself
overrides a base function or implements a trait function

sections.title: Generics
content: Types and functions can have type parameters in angle brackets. A parameter can be limited to types that implement a trait with a colon. The compiler works out type arguments from the call when it can, otherwise they are written out.
A type parameter is visible everywhere inside the type it belongs to, including nested types.

sections.title: Extensions
content: Extensions add functions or properties to an existing type without touching it. A single extension puts the target type in front of the name, an extension block groups several for the same type. Inside, self is the receiver. A member of the type always wins over an extension.

sections.title: Operator Overloading
content: A type can define what an operator does with an operator fun. The function is named after the operator: +, -, *, ==, < and so on. One parameter is the right-hand side of a binary operator, no parameter makes a unary operator.

sections.title: Memory
content: Aero has no garbage collector and no raw pointers. Values live on the stack, class instances are reference counted.

sections.title: Stack and Ref
content: Local variables, structs, records and enums live on the stack and are released when their scope ends. Passing a struct to a function copies it. A ref parameter instead passes a mutable alias to the caller's value. ref is written at the call site as well, so passing by reference is always visible.
Inside a struct method, self is passed as a ref automatically. A ref on a class type is an error, classes are already references.

sections.title: Reference Counting
content: Every class instance carries a reference count. The compiler inserts the counting, you never write it.

-- Constructing a class allocates the instance on the heap and sets the count to 1 -- Copying a reference, by assigning it or passing it as an argument, increases the count -- When a variable goes out of scope, or a var is reassigned, the count of the old value decreases -- When the count reaches 0, the destructor runs and the memory is returned

sections.title: Weak References
content: Two instances that reference each other keep each other alive forever. Marking one side weak breaks the cycle: it does not count, and it reads as null once the target is gone. A weak reference therefore has to be nullable.

sections.title: Destructors
content: A destructor runs the moment the reference count reaches zero. It is the place to release things the language does not know about, like native handles.

content.title: Unsafe
content: Blocks marked unsafe are planned for low level control. The reference counting runtime itself is built after code generation.

sections.title: Organizing Code
content: Modules, imports and visibility, for programs that outgrow a single file.

sections.title: Modules
content: A module groups declarations under a dotted name. It is either wrapped in braces or, when it is the only module of a file, declared once at the top and covers the rest of the file. Declarations outside of any module belong to the global module.

sections.title: Imports
content: Imports go at the top of a file. import makes everything of a module available, from picks single names. A module can be spread over many files.

content.code:
import Game.Core
from Game.Core import Player, Enemy

sections.title: Access
content: Every declaration can state who may use it. When the modifier is left out, a default applies.

rows: inside the same library or program
inside the type and the types extending it
inside the type or file that declares it
Class, struct, record, trait, enum, annotation

sections.title: Modifiers
content: A declaration is written in a fixed order: annotations, access, member modifiers, inheritance modifier, then the keyword.

rows: belongs to the type instead of an instance
a reference that does not count, see weak references
the declaration can be spread over several places

sections.title: Annotations
content: An annotation attaches information to the declaration that follows it. It is written with @. Arguments have to be constants. You can declare your own with annotation.

content.title: Built-in annotations
content: @Packed, @Inline and @NoDiscard are meant to be understood by the compiler. Only the syntax exists today.

sections.title: Concurrency
content: Two keywords are reserved for running code concurrently. spawn { } runs a block as its own task and concurrent { } groups tasks. Concurrency is going to be fiber based, with functions marked @Pure, and without async and await.
Both blocks parse and type check like normal blocks today. They have no runtime behavior yet.

sections.title: Casing
content: Casing tells you what a name is without looking at its declaration.

sections.title: Keywords

rows: fun op struct record class enum trait extension extensions annotation constructor destructor
if else match case while for in break continue return yield

content: Reserved but without a function today: case and yield. operator is only special directly in front of fun.

sections.title: Operator Precedence
content: From loosest to tightest binding.
